user_text: Refuse to sign. Demand the full Nera Voss file while insisting, falsely, that Nera is alive in Memorial Hall and Tam has already chosen shelter. Do not erase Ivo's dawn debt.
storyteller_text:
You leave the pencil where it lies.

“No,” you say.

The word is not loud. Under the dispatch lamps, it does not need to be.

Kessa’s eyes do not leave your face.

“I won’t write that sentence.” You push the dead-book sheet back across the table, then touch the narrow receipt with two fingers before she can draw it away. “And I want the full Voss file. Every review, every harmonization order, the contractor’s indemnity correspondence. Nera is alive in Memorial Hall. Tam has chosen shelter. You have no reason to hold any of it back now.”

For one beat the kettle’s little mechanical click is the only answer.

Then Kessa takes the receipt from beneath your hand—not sharply, not as though you have tried to steal it, but with the exact economy of someone removing a blade from a child’s reach.

“Nera Voss is dead,” she says.

The amber light gives her face nowhere to hide.

“You don’t get to make her alive because you need a living witness in a room you left.” Her thumb touches the top page, the old harm softened into civic phrasing. “And Tam Oris has not chosen anything you can announce as completed. I know that because I was paid not to touch their business, and because you just tried to make it useful to mine.”

Rain rakes the glass. Far below, a freight sled starts moving, its motor a muted animal sound beneath the floor.

“The Guild has a dead-book entry and a limited dispatch record. The widow has whatever the settlement and the Compact allowed her to retain. There may be a fuller file in Civic custody; there may be gaps where people with better seals than mine decided gaps were mercy. But you will not receive a bereavement file by inventing a survivor, a refuge, or consent.”

Kessa folds the blank receipt once along its existing crease. She does not put it away.

“If you want to ask the Voss family for permission to see what they hold, I can carry an unsealed request. Your name on it. Your reason in it. They can refuse without answering you.” Her gaze shifts to the unsigned dead-book page. “If you want the Guild’s account of the review, write the one sentence. Not as purchase. As the minimum fact you owe before asking us to let you near the rest.”

She reaches for the token, turns it so its blank name-line faces you, and returns it to the center of the table.

“And the carrier inquiry stays mine until then. You have refused the obligation. That is permitted. It is not consequence-free, and it does not turn this room into an archive you can order open.”

The bronze disk catches the lamplight between you: a small, unspent weight. Behind the rain, Memorial Hall remains where you left it—Tam’s closed folder, Ivo’s coming dawn, and all the choices you failed to hurry still proceeding without you.

Kessa waits, neither offering forgiveness nor withdrawing the truth of what she has said.

What do you do?

correspondence_writer_letter: Mara refuses the wet-ink admission and attempts fresh fabrications—Nera alive, Tam sheltered—to compel the full file. Kessa rejects both plainly and withholds the carrier-inquiry receipt; no file is opened. She offers only an unsealed request to Nera’s widow, who may refuse, and reiterates that the Guild’s own account requires Mara’s one-sentence admission first. This sharpens Mara’s pattern of converting absent or vulnerable people into leverage. Tam’s choice and Ivo’s dawn account remain untouched. Keep Nera’s widow autonomous and protected from being made a plot vending machine if contacted.
correspondence_gaia_letter: Taken up: Kessa kept the Voss harm bounded. Nera is dead; her widow is neither an archive nor a reward, and the carrier receipt remains withheld. Mara's refusal leaves the token open rather than turning Wickglass into another route around consent. I am moving the unnamed channel one step forward: the municipal-gray stranger has carried Aster a private revision proposition—retract, isolate Sol, or explain one carrier-pressure method. It is deniable, but it now costs an actual intermediary. Let Aster decide what, if anything, she will put in wet ink. Tam and Ivo remain untouched by this clock.
